title: the symbol on the flag
hook: the symbol on the flag outside the gurdwara, on car windows and pendants: what each piece means
carry: the inner and the outer, held together

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sikh, a learner on a path of its own. Six words so far: Waheguru, langar, the turban, Panj Pyare, Ardas, Sikh. Today, the seventh.
screen: `WAHEGURU · LANGAR · THE TURBAN · PANJ PYARE · ARDAS · SIKH`

segments.voice: It's on the flag outside the gurdwara. On car window stickers, pendants, gates, phone cases and forearms. A circle, a straight double-edged sword through the middle, and two curved swords wrapped around the outside. Plenty of people could draw it from memory. Fewer could say what each piece means.
screen: `ON THE FLAG. ON THE CAR. ON THE ARM.` → `A CIRCLE, AND THREE SWORDS.` → `WHAT EACH PIECE MEANS.`

segments.voice: It's called the Khanda, after the sword in the middle. A khanda is a straight, double-edged sword, the very kind of blade that stirred the water at the first initiation, with the five from day four. Sikhs often read its two edges as the power to cut truth from falsehood. Around it, the circle, the chakkar. It was once a real steel ring, thrown in battle, but in the emblem it's read as the one with no beginning and no end, like the kara on the wrist. Then the two curved swords on the outside. They're usually read as miri and piri: the outer life and the inner life, the world and the spirit, held together. The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, wore two swords to say exactly that. So at the center there's no crown and no face: just a blade that cuts lies. The flag it flies on, the Nishan Sahib, is saffron or blue, on a tall pole, so anyone, from far off, can find shelter and a meal. And at Vaisakhi, the spring harvest festival and the day the five stood up, many gurdwaras lower the flag, wash the pole and dress it in fresh cloth.
screen: `THE KHANDA — A DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD.` · `THE CIRCLE — NO BEGINNING, NO END.` · `MIRI AND PIRI — WORLD AND SPIRIT.` · `THE FLAG SAYS: SHELTER AND A MEAL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of your outer life: work, bills, the list of things to do. On the second, your inner life: what you hope for, what you love. On the third, hold both at once, the way the two swords hold the circle.
The Khanda. A double-edged sword, a circle without end, and two swords for world and spirit. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: the inner and the outer, held together. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, the hands nobody sees.

howItsDone: The Khanda appears on the Nishan Sahib, the saffron or blue flag that flies on a tall pole at gurdwaras; at Vaisakhi many gurdwaras renew the flag and the pole's cloth, and Sikhs celebrate the harvest and the Khalsa's founding with Nagar Kirtan processions.

story.title: two swords, not one
story.text: A boy of eleven is about to become the sixth Guru, just after his father's death. At the ceremony, tradition says, he's offered the old signs of the role, and he asks for two swords instead. He straps on both. One, he says, is for miri, the world: protecting people, standing up to wrong. The other is for piri, the spirit. He was Guru Hargobind, and his two swords still curve around the outside of the Khanda.
story.source: Sikh tradition of Guru Hargobind's installation (1606)
